work_order.root_cause: validateCapability answers TWO questions with one function, and only one of them is needed to be told the truth about a receipt. Its first three checks (MALFORMED_CAPABILITY shape, then BAD_SIGNATURE) answer IDENTITY: is this the envelope this server issued, unmoved? Its last three (EXPIRED_CAPABILITY, REPLAYED_NONCE, KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE) answer ADMISSION: may this envelope write NOW. A duplicate delivery arrives UNDER precisely the two conditions admission refuses - a spent nonce and often an active freeze - so identity could not simply be hoisted above the dedupe without breaking AC-2, and the ordering was resolved by leaving the dedupe where it was. src/executor/executor.js:199 reads repositories.actionRecords.getByNonce(capability.tenant, nonce) and returns {executed:false, duplicate:true, receipt_id, reconciliation, drift} before kernel.validateCapability runs at :231 and before the capabilities-table provenance lookup at :244. That lookup's answer describes the STORED envelope's mutation; the body that received it is described by the caller and was never authenticated. Because the lookup is keyed on `nonce` - a value the delivery itself carries - any body at all bearing a spent nonce is answered from the receipt table, and the receipt it is handed is the record of a different mutation. The two gates that would have caught it (the signature, and the comparison against the server's own stored envelope) both live strictly below the branch that returns.
work_order.understanding:
ATTEMPT 2's DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT AND ITS COVERAGE WAS NOT. Its root_cause is correct: a signed capability is not authority, the provenance lookup and the re-gate belong on the write path, and all five of QA's previous bugs are genuinely fixed - QA's own retest says so, one for one, and I did not find a sixth. What is wrong is that version 3 did not apply its own rule everywhere it applies. The rule was 'if a value decides whether money moves, exactly one function derives it, and every writer and reader calls that function.' It moved the receipt WRITER behind the gate. It left the receipt READER - the durable dedupe at executor.js:199 - above it, and that reader answers a question ('that mutation is already done, here is its receipt') from a value the caller supplied, having established nothing about the body it is talking to. One reader was audited; the other was not.

IT SAW THIS AND WROTE IT DOWN AS ACCEPTED. residual_risks(3) of version 3 says, in its own words: 'The duplicate short-circuit still runs before every check, so an unsigned POST naming a guessed nonce still learns a receipt id. That was the previous attempt's residual risk and it is deliberately unchanged, because AC-2 requires a duplicate made under a freeze to answer with its receipt.' The exposure is named accurately. The justification is a misreading of AC-2, and that misreading is the whole of BUG-6. AC-2 says: 'Delivering the same capability nonce twice performs the provider mutation exactly once; the second delivery answers 200 with executed:false, duplicate:true and the SAME receipt_id.' The subject is THE SAME ENVELOPE, delivered twice - a second tab, a retried POST. The plan widened it to 'any body carrying that nonce', then used the widened reading to justify leaving the gate below the branch. QA has now falsified exactly that widening, and it falsified it in both directions: the untampered re-delivery still answers 200 duplicate:true (AC-2 holds), and every other body bearing that nonce is now refused (the widening was never in the criterion). The kernel.js comment at :19-20 repeats the same slip in the same shape the plan diagnosed everywhere else - it asserts 'the write path proves provenance against the server's own capabilities table (executor.provenance)', naming a function that does not exist and stating a property that was true on one of the two paths through the write. A claim written in a comment is the artefact this repository keeps producing, and this time it was produced by the plan that named the artefact.

NO TEST COULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, AND THAT IS THE PATTERN TO RECORD. test/executor/executor.test.js:233 and :248 - the two cases that pin duplicate behaviour - build the duplicate by re-delivering the same object the test already spent, so the body under test is the server's own envelope by construction and the defect is unreachable from the suite. That is version 2's residual_risks(4) stated as a fact: 'checks whose fixtures are constructed by the same reasoning as the code they are meant to pin.' The Librarian entry is the one already written, with this as its second instance.

NOTHING HERE IS A CRITERION DEFECT, AND I CHECKED BEFORE SAYING SO. The code is wrong and the criteria are right, so AC-1 through AC-12 are carried forward word for word, unrenumbered and undropped, and AC-13 is added for the defect this PR's fix would otherwise leave open. The tempting move - rewriting AC-2 to say 'any body bearing a spent nonce is answered with that nonce's receipt' - is the worst artefact this pipeline can produce, because every future QA run would then certify the defect. I am not doing it. There is no internal contradiction in AC-2 to point at: 'the same capability nonce' is the same envelope, twice.

I REPRODUCED IT MYSELF against the branch build at df490b0, and the control that pins the cause is the same control QA found: the identical tamper on an UNSPENT nonce is already refused 403 BAD_SIGNATURE, so the mechanism works and is simply below the wrong branch. My outputs, not QA's, are in evidence[].
work_order.approach:
Do not add a check. SPLIT THE ONE CHECK INTO ITS TWO ANSWERS, and let the ordering fall out of the split rather than being argued about again. Every version of this plan so far has tried to fix a gap by adding a statement, and every gap has been a statement that was stated in the wrong place.

1. THE KERNEL OWNS TWO NAMED ANSWERS (src/policy/kernel.js). Extract verifyCapabilityIdentity(capability, { secret }) as its own exported pure function holding exactly the MALFORMED_CAPABILITY shape checks and the BAD_SIGNATURE comparison, and have validateCapability call it as its first step before it goes on to expiry, over-scope, replay and the kill switches. One implementation, two call sites - the same shape as version 3's revalidate port, and the same reason: a caller that assembles the check for itself is a caller that can stop calling it. createKernel binds it exactly as it binds validateCapability, so no caller in the repository ever hands a secret to a signing function by hand. The function's own comment states the boundary in one line: identity decides whether the server may TELL you something, admission decides whether you may WRITE, and the two conditions a duplicate arrives under - a spent nonce, a live freeze - belong to admission only.

2. THE EXECUTOR'S ORDER FOLLOWS (src/executor/executor.js). (0) tenant, unchanged. (1) IDENTITY: kernel.verifyCapabilityIdentity on the delivered body. (2) PROVENANCE: the existing capabilities-table lookup and stored-envelope comparison, moved up verbatim, with the STORED envelope acting as it already does from here on. (3) DURABLE DEDUPE: getByNonce, then the atomic claim, both where they are now but three checks lower. (4) ADMISSION: kernel.validateCapability - expiry, replay, kill switches - plus the existing re-gate, both below the dedupe and both before the provider is reached. Two consequences the implementer should not have to rediscover: the release() calls in the identity and provenance branches go away, because no claim is held yet (an unauthenticated body no longer takes the claim, which was a second, quieter exposure on the same branch), and the duplicate branch is now reachable only by a body the server has just proved is its own, so the receipt it returns describes that body by construction rather than by argument.

3. THE DEDUPE ANSWER IS PROVEN BY EQUALITY, NOT BY THE SIGNATURE ALONE. Widen ENVELOPE_FIELDS from ['authority','capability_id','signature'] to every field in kernel.SIGNED_FIELDS, so step (2) requires the delivered envelope to equal the stored one across everything issuance signed. The signature covers those fields today, so this changes no verdict; what it removes is the argument. With only three fields compared, correctness of the duplicate answer rested on the reader of the code knowing which fields the HMAC covers - and the same reader is what put the branch in the wrong place twice. One comparison, whole envelope, no reasoning left to do.

4. NOTHING AFTER THE DEDUPE MOVES. The re-gate and the kill-switch admission stay below it deliberately, and this is the line worth stating once: a delivery that will not write is answered from storage, and a delivery that will write passes every check. That is why a duplicate of a genuine envelope is still answered 200 under a freeze - the operator must not be told their action failed when it succeeded - while any other body is refused before the freeze is even consulted. I applied exactly this shape to the branch and measured it: 425/425 tests pass including the two duplicate cases, and the six repro bodies go 403 while the untampered one stays 200 both with and without a freeze.

5. TWO COMMENTS THAT ARE NOW LOAD-BEARING. The executor's module header already carries an ordered list of the checks and states that the order IS the safety property; renumber it so it describes the path in the file, and fix the kernel.js comment at :19-20 that names a non-existent executor.provenance and claims a property the file did not have. A comment that asserts a safety property is a test nobody runs, and this repository has now been bitten by one twice.

`src/strategy/guardian.js:285`

Evidence: Two-run reproduction against a clean seeded DB (PORT=3112, DB_PATH=/tmp/i20c/app.db), following the work order's qa_script. RUN 1: step 2 mints and executes campaign-status on campaign_001 -> 200. Step 6 raises a global freeze; step 7 re-enables global (200) and raises a campaign_007 freeze. Step 13's `POST /v1/guardian/re-enable {"actor":"owner"}` -> 409 NO_ACTIVE_FREEZE (the provider row was already clear), then the step-0 reset prints 'seed --reset-approvals: purged 0 receipts, released 0 claims, 3 approvals pending, 1 lapsed, 1 kill switch cleared (provider meta_ads)'. RUN 2 on that 'reset' database: `curl -sS /approvals | grep -c guardian-banner` -> 1 (a clean step 0 must show 0); a fresh campaign-status capability on campaign_007 -> 409 KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE after the reset; and `GET /v1/guardian` still lists the campaign row active. The reset is also the printed summary's own contract — the work order's qa_script step 0 requires the line to name 'kill switches cleared', and it names one row while another is still frozen. Test coverage asserts only the provider case: test/data/seed.test.js:116 and :250 both call `repositories.killSwitches.upsertFreeze({scope:'provider', scope_id:'meta_ads', ...})` by hand, so `activeFor(...).length === 0` at :128 and :265 passes without ever exercising a non-provider key — the same fixture-supplies-the-value shape the work order's understanding names as this repository's characteristic failure. Note the pre-fix build behaves the same way at the reset (a global freeze also survives it, under key global/meta_ads), so this is not a new regression; it is a pre-existing gap that BUG-3's fix newly made reachable, because until this PR no route could write a non-provider row that a later run would depend on.

Fix: Derive the cleared rows from the same roster the writer uses rather than from one literal pair — iterate FREEZE_SCOPES and call killSwitches.isActive/reEnable for each canonical key (freezeScopeId already returns the id for global/tenant/provider; the campaign key is not derivable from a tenant alone, so read repositories.killSwitches.listForTenant(tenantId) and clear every active row for the tenant, or clear the three derivable keys plus any active campaign rows). Then report the count of rows actually cleared rather than a constant 1. Add a test that upserts a global and a campaign-scoped row through guardian.freeze and asserts the reset leaves activeFor empty for all four scopes — the existing provider-only fixture cannot fail.
